title: Mist or rain?
opening_question: What watered the ground before the flood, and what does the text say about rain?

steps.question: What did God make on Day 2, and what did it divide?

facts.text: "Firmament" is the Hebrew raqia: "properly an expanse". God made it between waters: "the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament".

steps.question: Why had no plant grown yet, and what watered the ground?

facts.text: "Mist" is the Hebrew 'ed: "a fog"; the KJV translates it "mist" and "vapor". It stands only twice in the Bible: here and in Job 36:27.
The translations differ here. The KJV says "there went up a mist from the earth", the Ethiopian Canon "a mist went up from the earth"; the BSB says "springs welled up from the earth".

Genesis 2:5 gives two reasons no plant had grown yet: "the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground". It speaks of the time before the plants and before Adam. The text does not say whether it rained between then and the flood.

steps.question: The word for "mist" is used only twice. What does the other verse say about it?

facts.text: In Job 36:27 the KJV translates the same word 'ed as "vapour": rain falls "according to the vapour thereof". The BSB: "distill the rain from the mist". Here mist and rain stand in one sentence.

steps.question: Where did the flood waters come from, and how long did it rain?

facts.text: The waters came from below and above at once: "all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened". "Deep" is tehom: "an abyss (as a surging mass of water)".
Genesis 7:4 uses the same Hebrew verb as Genesis 2:5 (matar, "to rain"): "I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights".
"Flood" is mabbul: "a deluge". Every time but one it means Noah's flood; the other is Psalm 29:10: "The LORD sitteth upon the flood".
Peter looks back on the same event: "the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished".

steps.question: What did God set in the cloud, and what is it a token of?

facts.text: "Bow" is qesheth: "a bow for shooting". The rainbow and the archer's bow are one word in Hebrew.
God says the bow is also for Him to see: "I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant".
The text calls the bow "a token of a covenant". It does not say whether a rainbow had ever been seen before.

steps.question: Where are waters still spoken of, and what was Noah warned about?

facts.text: Psalm 148, written long after the flood, still speaks of "waters that be above the heavens".

remember.text: "the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth" ... "there went up a mist from the earth"
The fountains of the great deep were broken up and the windows of heaven were opened.
"I do set my bow in the cloud"
Noah was "warned of God of things not seen as yet".
